summary: Describes using the Camellia block cipher in CBC, CTR and CCM modes as additional, optional-to-implement mechanisms for IKEv2 and ESP in IPsec. They provide confidentiality and, in the case of CCM, integrity.

eli5.summary: IPsec locks internet traffic, and this note adds another lock called Camellia as an optional choice, with several ways to use it.

questions: how to use camellia with ipsec

subtitle: How the Camellia cipher plugs into IPsec as an optional alternative, in CBC, CTR and CCM modes.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs a choice of encryption algorithms, and Camellia, a 128-bit block cipher, had no defined way to be used in IKEv2 and ESP in three common modes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC points to existing definitions for Camellia in CBC, CTR and CCM modes, says how much keying material IKEv2 must produce for each, and records the IANA transform numbers 23 to 27.
tldr.outcome: Implementers get optional-to-implement Camellia transforms that give confidentiality and, with CCM, data origin authentication and connectionless integrity.

today: RFC 5529 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its transforms are optional to implement.

sections.title: What the RFC Adds to IPsec
sections.content:
RFC 5529 describes the use of the Camellia block cipher in three modes of operation: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC), Counter (CTR) and Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM). They are defined as additional, optional-to-implement mechanisms for IKEv2 and for the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

The goals are confidentiality, data origin authentication and connectionless integrity. The RFC says that optimized source code for Camellia is available under several open source licenses, and that OpenSSL, FreeBSD, Linux and Firefox Gran Paradiso adopted it. It refers readers to RFC 4301 and RFC 4303 for how the pieces of IPsec fit together.
sections.eli5: IPsec already has some locks. This note says here is one more lock, Camellia, that you may use if you want to.

sections.title: The Camellia Cipher: Block Size and Padding
sections.content:
The RFC does not describe the cipher itself. It says the relevant characteristics, such as key size and rounds, are described in RFC 3713. What it does state is that Camellia uses a block size of 16 octets (128 bits).

Padding is not redefined either. For plain Camellia, for Camellia-CBC and for ESP in general, the requirement is in RFC 4303. For Camellia-CCM it is in NIST Special Publication 800-38C. On performance, the RFC only points to the Camellia web site and to the independent NESSIE project report.
sections.eli5: Camellia chops data into 16-byte pieces. This note does not repeat how the cipher works. It just tells you which other documents to read.

sections.title: The Three Modes
sections.content:
Three modes are supported for Camellia with IPsec: CBC, CTR and CCM. The RFC defines none of them from scratch.

  • Camellia CBC mode is defined in RFC 4312.
  • Camellia in CTR and CCM modes is used in IPsec the same way AES is, following RFC 3686 for CTR and RFC 4309 for CCM.
  • For CCM, the Camellia block cipher itself is the one from RFC 5528.

So the work here is mostly wiring: reuse the AES-style rules and swap in Camellia.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to use the lock. The note says to do it just like the AES lock people already know, only with a Camellia lock inside.

sections.title: Keying Material in IKEv2
sections.content:
IKEv2 produces KEYMAT, a block of key bytes for each security association. The RFC requires that KEYMAT MUST be equal to or longer than the associated Camellia key, and then says how many octets to request per mode.

  • CBC: 16, 24 or 32 octets for 128, 192 or 256-bit keys. All of it is the Camellia key.
  • CTR: 20, 28 or 36 octets. The first 16, 24 or 32 are the key and the last four octets are the nonce value in the counter block.
  • CCM: 19, 27 or 35 octets. The first 16, 24 or 32 are the key and the last three octets are the salt value in the counter block.
sections.eli5: When two computers agree on a secret, they get a pile of random bytes. The note says which bytes are the key and which few are extra pieces that go into the counter.

sections.title: Transform Type and Key Length
sections.content:
In an IKEv2 negotiation, Camellia is offered as an ESP encryption transform (Transform Type 1). IANA assigned five transform identifiers for it.

Camellia supports three key lengths, so the Key Length attribute MUST be specified in the IKE exchange, and it MUST have a value of 128, 192 or 256 bits.
sections.eli5: When two computers set up their lock, they must say how big the key is: 128, 192 or 256 bits. They cannot leave it out.

sections.title: IANA Transform Numbers
sections.content:
IANA assigned these values for Transform Type 1 (Encryption Algorithm):

  • 23 for ENCR_CAMELLIA_CBC
  • 24 for ENCR_CAMELLIA_CTR
  • 25 for ENCR_CAMELLIA_CCM with an 8-octet ICV
  • 26 for ENCR_CAMELLIA_CCM with a 12-octet ICV
  • 27 for ENCR_CAMELLIA_CCM with a 16-octet ICV

CCM gets three numbers because the integrity check value (ICV) can have three lengths.
sections.eli5: Each way of using the lock gets its own number so computers can name it. CCM gets three because its stamp can be three sizes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This RFC does not analyze security in depth. For CTR and CCM it refers to Section 9 of RFC 3686 and Section 7 of RFC 4309. It also states that no security problem has been found for Camellia, citing the CRYPTREC evaluation and the NESSIE project.
sections.eli5: The note says the safety rules are written in other documents, and so far nobody has found a way to break Camellia.
